\section[il malinteso]{il malinteso — the misunderstanding}

\label{lesson:IT-C346-malinteso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for credible, then the Italian for reliable.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il malinteso}
\textbf{il malinteso} — \textquotedblleft{}the misunderstanding\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi dispiace, è stato un malinteso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am sorry, it was a misunderstanding.}
\end{quote}

\emph{C'è stato un malinteso} — there has been a misunderstanding.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{malinteso} is built from \emph{male} \textquotedblleft{}badly\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{male}, and \emph{inteso}, past participle of \emph{intendere} \textquotedblleft{}to understand\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{intendere} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch towards, to direct the mind\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{tendere}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il malinteso}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il malinteso}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il malinteso}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for credible, then the Italian for reliable, then say \emph{il malinteso} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il malinteso mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The misunderstanding\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fraintendere]{fraintendere — to misunderstand}

\label{lesson:IT-C346-fraintendere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for reliable, then the Italian for the misunderstanding.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fraintendere}
\textbf{fraintendere} — \textquotedblleft{}to misunderstand\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Forse mi hai frainteso: non volevo criticarti.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Maybe you misunderstood me: I did not want to criticise you.}
\end{quote}

Past participle \emph{frainteso}. Built like \emph{intendere}, which means to understand.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fraintendere} is built from \emph{fra} \textquotedblleft{}between, partly\textquotedblright{} and \emph{intendere} \textquotedblleft{}to understand\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{intendere} \textquotedblleft{}to direct the mind\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{tendere} \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}: to understand halfway.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fraintendere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fraintendere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fraintendere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for reliable, then the Italian for the misunderstanding, then say \emph{fraintendere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does fraintendere mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To misunderstand\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chiarire]{chiarire — to clarify, to clear up}

\label{lesson:IT-C346-chiarire}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the misunderstanding, then the Italian for to misunderstand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: chiarire}
\textbf{chiarire} — \textquotedblleft{}to clarify, to clear up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Vorrei chiarire una cosa prima di cominciare.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I would like to clarify one thing before we start.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated with \emph{-isc-}: \emph{chiarisco, chiarisci}. \emph{Chiarirsi} — to sort things out with someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{chiarire} is built on \emph{chiaro} \textquotedblleft{}clear\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{clārus} \textquotedblleft{}bright, loud, clear\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to make something clear.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chiarire}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{chiarire}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the misunderstanding, then the Italian for to misunderstand, then say \emph{chiarire} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[precisare]{precisare — to specify, to make clear (a detail)}

\label{lesson:IT-C346-precisare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to misunderstand, then the Italian for to clarify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: precisare}
\textbf{precisare} — \textquotedblleft{}to specify, to make clear (a detail)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Voglio precisare che non è colpa mia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I want to make clear that it is not my fault.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ci tengo a precisare che} — I want to point out that. Built on \emph{preciso} \textquotedblleft{}precise\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{precisare} is built on \emph{preciso} \textquotedblleft{}precise\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{praecīsus} \textquotedblleft{}cut off, abrupt\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{praecīdere} \textquotedblleft{}to cut off in front\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{caedere} \textquotedblleft{}to cut\textquotedblright{}: what is left after cutting away the extra.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\section[il chiarimento]{il chiarimento — the clarification, the explanation}

\label{lesson:IT-C346-chiarimento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to clarify, then the Italian for to specify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il chiarimento}
\textbf{il chiarimento} — \textquotedblleft{}the clarification, the explanation\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ho chiesto un chiarimento al professore.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I asked the teacher for a clarification.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Chiedere un chiarimento} — to ask for a clarification. Between friends it can also be a frank talk that sorts things out.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{chiarimento} is built on \emph{chiarire} \textquotedblleft{}to clarify\textquotedblright{} with the noun ending \emph{-mento}; the verb comes from \emph{chiaro}, inherited from Latin \emph{clārus} \textquotedblleft{}bright, clear\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il chiarimento}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il chiarimento}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il chiarimento}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to clarify, then the Italian for to specify, then say \emph{il chiarimento} again
\end{itemize}
